entries.title: Germany's long road to equality for same-sex couples
entries.summary: In 2001, same-sex couples in Germany were able to register a civil partnership for the first time. The Civil Partnership Act was a crucial step toward "marriage for all," which was introduced in 2017.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany's long road to equality for same-sex couples

August 1, 2026

In 2001, same-sex couples in Germany were able to register a civil partnership for the first time. The Civil Partnership Act was a crucial step toward "marriage for all," which was introduced in 2017.

August 1, 2001, marked a turning point: with the Civil Partnership Act, same-sex couples in Germany gained a legal framework for the registration of their partnerships. However, another 16 years would pass before marriage itself became an option.

"The Civil Partnership Act was a milestone for the legal recognition of same-sex couples in Germany and laid the foundation for opening up marriage," Alexander Vogt of the national board of "Queere Vielfalt e.V." (Queer diversity) told DW.

"It introduced a legally secure partnership with rights similar to those of marriage — such as inheritance, maintenance, and residency rights — though it remained discriminatory in many areas – like adoption or tax law. Nevertheless, it gave us a foot in the door — a solid base from which further rights could be secured, usually by appealing to the Federal Constitutional Court."

Public opinion was ahead of the political establishment

The legislation was preceded by a fierce political debate. The opposition bloc of conservative parties, the Christian Democratic Union and the Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), denounced it as an "unconstitutional attack on marriage and the family." Lawmakers from the ruling center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), however, described the law as "a long-overdue act of redress."

"There was strong conservative opposition, for instance from churches and civic groups," Alexander Vogt noted. "The debate reflected the classic culture war between traditional and progressive values."

Backed by the governing coalition of Social Democrats and Greens, the majority of Bundestag lawmakers voted in favor of the Civil Partnership Act in November 2000, despite opposition from the CDU/CSU and the neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP).

German public opinion was already a step ahead: A 1999 survey showed that 55% of respondents were already in favor of the Civil Partnership Act.

However, Germany was by no means a pioneer. Denmark was the first country in the world to introduce civil partnerships for same-sex couples, doing so as early as 1989. Norway, Sweden, and Iceland followed in the mid-1990s, with France following in 1999.

'We simply wanted equal treatment'

Twenty-five years ago, Reinhard Lüschow and his husband Heinz-Friedrich Harre — who has since passed away — became the first same-sex couple in Germany to tie the knot at a registry office under the new Civil Partnership Act. They had spent the preceding decade fighting for legal recognition as a couple.

As early as 1992, they had made a public statement by applying to register their marriage — in a coordinated move by 250 male and female same-sex couples across Germany. When their application was rejected, they took the case all the way to the Federal Constitutional Court. "We simply wanted to be treated equally," Lüschow recently told the Protestant Press Service (epd).

Although the court ruled at the time that marriage was a union between a man and a woman, it also mandated that the legislature ensure same-sex partnerships were not discriminated against. When the Bundestag implemented this requirement through the Civil Partnership Act, Lüschow and Harre reacted immediately.

Hard-won changes

The Civil Partnership Act regulates matters such as the use of surnames, mutual financial support, and inheritance rights. In the years that followed, the scope of civil partnerships was gradually expanded — first in 2004 to include stepchild adoption, and later to achieve tax equality following several rulings by the Federal Constitutional Court.

The Civil Partnership Act was merely the first step toward equality. The decisive step did not come until October 1, 2017, with legislation that introduced so-called "marriage for all."

This, too, was a hard-won victory. The conservative parties had come to power again in 2005. They blocked the legislation until Chancellor Angela Merkel authorized a vote free from party-line constraints, meaning lawmakers were to follow only their consciences; this is how the majority was secured in 2017. Angela Merkel and current Chancellor Friedrich Merz voted against the legislation.

Bodo Mende and Karl Kreile were the first same-sex couple to marry. Reflecting on the 2001 Civil Partnership Act, Mende later told DW: "It was a second-class partnership." Although there were few legal restrictions, the status lacked the standing of a conventional marriage.

Married partners enjoy more rights — for instance, regarding naming laws, child adoption, and the equalization of pension rights. Marriage also carries greater recognition internationally.

According to the Federal Statistical Office, around 108,000 couples had availed themselves of this new option by 2025. At the same time, approximately 24,000 registered civil partnerships remain in existence; these can be converted into marriages upon application.

'Marriage for all' does not amount to full equality

Differences remain between same-sex and opposite-sex couples. Alexander Vogt of the association Queere Vielfalt cites an example regarding the law of parentage: "If a child is born into a family with two mothers, the non-biological mother must first go through an adoption process to establish legal parenthood. This is not the case for heterosexual couples."

Reflecting on societal developments, Vogt observes: "Acceptance of same-sex marriage has clearly increased."

However, he adds: "We have become more visible in recent years, but not safer; violence and hate crimes — particularly against queer people — have risen sharply. The figures have increased tenfold since 2010! The attack in Berlin represents a tragic peak in this trend, one that has garnered significant public attention."

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Germany widens deportations to Afghanistan
entries.summary: Earlier this week, Germany for the first time deported a man with no criminal record to Kabul. Faridoon Tofan, who is currently in deportation detention, fears the same fate.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany widens deportations to Afghanistan

August 1, 2026

Earlier this week, Germany for the first time deported a man with no criminal record to Kabul. Faridoon Tofan, who is currently in deportation detention, fears the same fate.

Things would likely have turned out very differently had Faridoon Tofan not taken the bus to Italy. He had intended to go on a short trip to Rome. The 46-year-old — who had fled the Taliban to Germany just under four years ago and had since been working and learning the language — was detained during a border check in mid-April and taken directly to a deportation detention center in Munich.

The reason: Tofan did not have the legal right to leave Germany. His asylum application had been rejected; he held only a temporary residence permit, which does not protect against deportation. He could now be sent back to Kabul, even though he is neither a convicted criminal nor has he been classified as a security threat. His asylum application appeal was definitively rejected in July, and he is now to be deported.

Tofan's wife and six children are still living in Kabul. They were recently paid a visit by Taliban officials and say they've been living in constant fear ever since and the sons no longer dare attend school, Nina Alizadeh Marandi told DW. She is an asylum law expert at the human rights organization Amnesty International in Germany and in close contact with Tofan's lawyer.

The Taliban officials' interest in the Tofan family in Kabul came after Faridoon Tofan's meeting with Afghan consulate staff in Berlin. Both the embassy in the German capital and the Afghan Consulate General in Bonn are now under Taliban control — a state of affairs for which the German government has faced heavy criticism from the opposition and human rights organizations.

While the German government does not officially recognize the Taliban administration as the legitimate government of Afghanistan, it points to contacts maintained at a purely "technical level."

Deportation precedent

This week, another Afghan national with no criminal record was deported.

The flight — operated by Freebird Airlines using an Airbus A320-214 — departed Leipzig/Halle Airport in Eastern Germany at 1:43 a.m. on Tuesday, bound for Trabzon, Turkey, before continuing to Kabul, Afghanistan. The Afghan national with no criminal record was on the plane alongside 30 convicted offenders.

This set a precedent that sparked vociferous protests: 260 people heeded the call of an anti-racism alliance and came to demonstrate inside the airport's departure hall, accompanied by a police escort.

Luca Müller, spokesperson for the anti-racism group, also referenced the deadly terror attack on the Pride event in Berlin over the weekend: "While Islamist violence targeting Berlin's Pride celebration is being condemned from all sides, the federal government is supporting the Islamist Taliban through its deals," Müller said.

By "deals," Müller is referring to accusations leveled by many human rights organizations and the political opposition that the German government is de facto legitimizing the Taliban regime in Afghanistan in order to facilitate more deportations.

Interior Minister justifies the tough approach

What critics view as a breach of fundamental taboo, others see as nothing more than the swift enforcement of existing law. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt again told journalists this week, that anyone who has gone through an asylum process resulting in a rejection is therefore required to leave the country and must expect deportation if they do not depart voluntarily. Dobrindt, who is a member of Bavaria's conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), stated that the federal government is simply pursuing its goals in migration policy, driving forward this "shift in migration policy" with "control, a clear course, and a firm stance," Dobrindt added.

Improved security situation in Afghanistan?

Since the resumption of deportations to Afghanistan in 2024, Germany has returned more than 200 individuals. According to Amnesty International, at least one of them was killed following his arrival in Kabul.

However, the German government points to assessments by the UN migration agency (IOM), which considers the return of men to Afghanistan to be feasible again — in principle.

"The security situation in Afghanistan has improved significantly; that is simply an objective fact," Mihyung Park, the IOM's country chief in Kabul, told the media outlet Redaktionsnetzwerk Deutschland. Park added one caveat: "Under current circumstances, we would strongly advise women against returning to Afghanistan."

In general, however, UN agencies warn against involuntary returns, noting that the returnees heavily depend on support to settle again in their country of origin.

Amnesty International condemns the German government for increasingly toughening its deportation practices without regard for the catastrophic human rights situation in Afghanistan. Nina Alizadeh Marandi pointed out that the very day of this week's historical deportation happened to coincide with the 75th anniversary of the adoption of the Geneva Refugee Convention.

"Human rights standards must not be eroded simply because upholding them is politically inconvenient," Alizadeh Marandi said. "Amnesty calls on the federal government to refrain from further deportations and to monitor whether Afghans who have already been deported are able to live in Afghanistan without persecution or danger to life and limb," she added.

Opposition speaks of a 'dangerous wrong turn'

Germany's political opposition has also sharply criticized the first deportation of an Afghan national with no criminal record. "It is irresponsible that Alexander Dobrindt is now deporting people to Afghanistan who have done absolutely nothing wrong here," said Marcel Emmerich, the Green Party's parliamentary spokesperson on interior policy.

Emmerich said that Dobrindt's "dirty deal" regarding deportations strengthens the Taliban, "makes us vulnerable to blackmail, and undermines Germany's own security." He added that the federal government is taking a "dangerous wrong turn" with this Afghanistan policy.

Juliane Nagel, a lawmaker for the socialist Left Party in the parliament of the eastern state of Saxony, called the flight "shameful" and demanded that Saxony's Leipzig/Halle Airport — which is largely state-owned — no longer be used for deportations to Afghanistan.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Famed climber Nirmal Purja among 10 killed in avalanche
entries.summary: A major search was launched after an avalanche struck the expedition high on Pakistan's Broad Peak. The confirmation ended hopes of a rescue and marked the loss of one of the world's best-known high-altitude climbers.
entries.content:
August 1, 2026

A major search was launched after an avalanche struck the expedition high on Pakistan's Broad Peak. The confirmation ended hopes of a rescue and marked the loss of one of the world's best-known high-altitude climbers.

Celebrated climber Nirmal Purja and nine other mountaineers have been confirmed dead after an avalanche on Pakistan's Broad Peak, his expedition company said on Saturday.

The confirmation came a day after rescuers located four bodies while searching for the 10-member expedition.

How did Purja and the other mountaineers die?

"It is with profound sadness and immense heartbreak that we confirm that Nirmal Purja tragically lost his life following the avalanche on Broad Peak," Purja's company Elite Expeditions said in a social media post.

"We have also received confirmation that other members of the expedition sadly did not survive."

The climbers had been missing since Thursday, when an avalanche struck the expedition at around 6,600 meters (21,650 feet) on Broad Peak. The party is believed to have been swept away.

Two Pakistan Army Aviation helicopters joined the operation on Friday, while an experienced ground team was deployed to the area where the group was last believed to have been.

Pakistani security sources said four bodies had been located that day, although they had not yet been recovered.

At the time, rescuers were still searching for the remaining members of the group.

The deaths of all 10 climbers were confirmed on Saturday.

The expedition included Purja and five other Nepalese climbers, including several Sherpa guides, as well as mountaineers from four other countries.

They were Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi, Omani climber Nathira Ahmed, US climber Mallory Geis and China's Wang Zhong.

Who was Nirmal Purja?

Nirmal Purja, widely known as Nims Dai, was a British-Nepali mountaineer who became one of the best-known high-altitude climbers of his generation.

The 43-year-old served with Britain's Brigade of Gurkhas and later the elite Special Boat Service before leaving the military to become a full-time mountaineer and guide.

Purja shot to international fame in 2019 when he climbed all 14 of the world's mountains above 8,000 meters in just over six months, dramatically beating the previous record of nearly eight years.

His feat was chronicled in the 2021 Netflix documentary "14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible," which helped bring him a global following.

In 2021, Purja was also part of the 10-member Nepali team that completed the first winter ascent of K2, the world's second-highest mountain.

Before the latest ascent, Purja had posted his hopes for the expedition on X, asking the mountain for safe passage.

What is Broad Peak?

Broad Peak stands at just over 8,000 meters in Pakistan's Karakoram range, close to the border with China. It is the world's 12th-highest mountain and lies only a few kilometers from the better-known K2.

Originally designated K3 during the surveying of the Karakoram, its more modern name refers to its unusually wide summit ridge, which stretches for roughly 1.5 kilometers (just under a mile).

The region contains five of the world's 14 peaks above 8,000 meters and attracts climbers from across the globe, although avalanches and rapidly changing weather make expeditions particularly dangerous.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic, Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: More women die in heatwaves, but biology 'isn't main cause'
entries.summary: In country after country, more women are dying from the heat than men. But researchers say biology isn't the main reason. Age, working conditions, and unequal access to rest may drive the gap.
entries.content:
ScienceGlobal issues

More women die in heatwaves, but biology 'isn't main cause'

August 1, 2026

In country after country, more women are dying from the heat than men. But researchers say biology isn't the main reason. Age, working conditions, and unequal access to rest may drive the gap.

Observing recent heatwaves in Europe, one pattern has often been remarked on: More women appear to be dying than men. During Europe's then-record summer of 2022, a study found 56% more heat-related deaths among women than men, drawing on mortality data from 35 countries.

Germany, which has just logged its deadliest heat season since 2016, with close to 9,800 heat-related deaths by mid-July, according to the Robert Koch Institute, is seeing the same pattern again this year.

Are hormones making heatwaves more dangerous for women?

Some of the recent coverage has leaned on the hormonal reading that women's bodies simply aren't equipped for heat. They sweat less, carry more body fat, and progesterone nudges core temperature up. 

But scientists who study the effect of heat on the human body say that's largely incorrect. "Overall, studies usually show only slightly more vulnerability to heat in women compared to men," saidAlexandra Schneider, an environmental epidemiologist and deputy director of the Institute of Epidemiology at Helmholtz Munich. "It's not really a very strong signal."

The small differences that do exist are real: Women do have a lower sweat rate, less skin area relative to body size, and fat distribution that affects thermoregulation. Hormones play a role too, but unevenly across a lifetime.

Schneider points to one group in particular: Women past menopause, when cardiovascular risk climbs. Older women with existing heart disease, she says, are probably at the highest risk of all.

But even in those cases, she doesn't think biology is the main cause for the extra deaths during a heatwave. "The living conditions, the social environment where women live, makes probably even more of a risk than just the differences in hormone status."

A research gap, not a biological difference

Toby Mündel, a kinesiology professor at Brock University in Canada, who studies extreme human environments, says that the impact is "overstated," when asked whether there's a real biological basis for the claim that women are more likely to die in heatwaves.

The factors that most determine how a person copes with a heatwave, Mündel says, are age, body size, fitness and habitual activity, and not biological sex.

Sweating is one example. Even though women do sweat less, that doesn't make them more vulnerable, because they compensate in another way. "They send blood flow to the skin, vasodilation, much better than males do," Mündel says, meaning their blood vessels widen more efficiently, moving heat to the surface where it can escape.

Pregnancy, which many assume must be dangerous, is another example. "As a woman progresses through pregnancy, she actually becomes better at handling heat," Mündel says. He draws a clear line between physiology and circumstance: There are good reasons not to have pregnant women doing heavy outdoor labor in extreme heat. But their bodies aren't the reason.

Why does the data suggest otherwise?

Partly, Mündel's argument is based on what gets measured. Studies often count hospital and emergency admissions, and women are far more likely than men to seek medical help. "That is not a physiological thing," he says. "Are they actually struggling, or have they just sought help earlier?"

Underneath it all sits a research gap. "We have about a hundred times as much data and evidence on men. We have nearly zero on women," Mündel says. "It's like comparing cats and dogs."

Numbers from Germany point in the same direction. The Robert Koch Institute attributes the higher female death toll to the fact that women make up a larger share of the oldest age groups. Its estimates also break down deaths per 100,000 people, and by that measure, the picture flips.

In every older age band this summer, the male death rate is higher than the female one. In other words, more women are dying in heatwaves only because more very old women are alive.

The real risk is exposure for women, not biology

If the gap isn't physiological, where does it come from?

Laurie Parsons, a researcher at Royal Holloway, University of London, studieshow heat stress moves through the global economy in construction, garment factories, farming, driving, street vending.

Across the board, he says, women spend 30% to 50% more of their working time above heat-stress thresholds than men. In construction, when comparing men and women doing the same job, the figure rises to around 50%.

The reasons, he says, are structural. Women often wear more clothing for the same job. Men are more confident asking for breaks. And where men's work is visibly strenuous, it's recognized as a heat risk and rewarded with rest. But women's work is steadier, less obviously punishing, and gets no such relief.

Parsons compares it to the difference between a plane crash and asbestos exposure: One is a sudden, visible catastrophe, the other a slow, constant harm that's easy to miss. "Male heat stress tends to be this taller risk, where you get relatively visible moments of physical distress that can be managed," he says. "Female heat stress is constantly there, but much less visible, because it doesn't have those same obvious peaks in the working day."

Then the shift ends, he says. Men rest, but women cook, clean and care for children.

Heat also cuts into pay. Parsons says workers under heat stress are around 30% less productive in the garment sector, which he says is the easiest to quantify.

In formal jobs, workers make up for it with longer hours during the hottest part of the day, feeding what he calls "a vicious cycle" of worsening health and falling output. The self-employed have no such buffer. For them, heat stress just means less income, which ripples the wider family over time.

For Parsons, the starting premise is flawed. "Heat stress is not an atmospheric condition," he says. "It is a social condition, which happens within particular atmospheric circumstances."

Edited by Ben Knight

entries.title: Iran warns neighbors against being US 'defensive shield'
entries.summary: Iran has warned regional states against helping the US as Washington weighs possible "very hard" new strikes. Meanwhile, the Tehran-backed Houthis claim to have diverted eight Saudi tankers from the Red Sea. DW has more.
entries.content:
Iran

Iran warns neighbors against being US 'defensive shield'

Published August 1, 2026last updated August 1, 2026

Iran has warned regional states against helping the US as Washington weighs possible "very hard" new strikes. Meanwhile, the Tehran-backed Houthis claim to have diverted eight Saudi tankers from the Red Sea. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Tehran said any country acting as a shield for the US could be drawn into the war
  • Donald Trump has threatened to hit Iran 'very hard,' with US reports pointing to possible strikes on energy infrastructure
  • The Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen claim to have diverted eight Saudi oil tankers around South Africa's Cape of Good Hope

Read below for all the latest headlines on the Iran war on Saturday, Aug 1, 2026.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Israel claims to have killed several Hezbollah fighters

Israel claims to have killed several Hezbollah fighters

Israel's military on Saturday said its forces killed several Hezbollah fighters in southern Lebanon. A post on the military's official X account said that one of its combat officers was injured during the armed encounter and had been hospitalized.

The post pledged that the Israeli military would "continue to operate to remove any threat its forces and will not allow the Hezbollah terror organization to harm the citizens of the state of Israel."

The incident came despite a ceasefire being in place between Israel and the Iranian-backed militants. While Hezbollah has formally denounced the deal, the group has not claimed any attacks since theUS-sponsored framework agreement was signed by Israel and Lebanon and then put in place in late June.

The agreement remains fragile, with Hezbollah refusing to disarm and Israel refusing to leave southern Lebanon — both points outlined in the agreement.

Despite the relative decline in violence in southern Lebanon, Israel has continued to conduct airstrikes and carry out other military operations.

Lebanon has condemned Israel's operations, saying that its continued military operations make it impossible to fully deploy the Lebanese army as outlined in the deal.

Skip next section US urges citizens to prepare to leave Middle East

US urges citizens to prepare to leave Middle East

US embassies across the Middle East have urged US nationals to consider leaving the region or be ready to depart if the conflict escalates further.

"Americans in the region should consider departing, or be prepared to depart should there be escalation," security alerts posted by US missions in Amman, Jerusalem and Baghdad said.

The warnings told citizens to check flight information, follow local safety instructions and prepare for cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruption.

Those in Jordan were advised to stay away from US military bases, which have recently come under Iranian missile attack.

In Israel, US citizens were urged to identify the nearest bomb shelter.

"The Iranian regime is unpredictable," the US Embassy in Jerusalem said, citing recent attacks across the region and an expansion to areas not previously targeted, including Egypt.

A drone struck a US-owned gas vessel moored at an Egyptian port on Wednesday, sparking a fire. Egyptian authorities are investigating and have not publicly blamed any group.

Skip next section New attacks hit Kuwait and Strait of Hormuz shipping

New attacks hit Kuwait and Strait of Hormuz shipping

Kuwait's military says it is responding to a fresh wave of Iranian drone attacks that struck several "vital facilities" in the country.

Defense Ministry spokesperson Maj. Gen. Saud Abdulaziz Al-Otaibi said the targets included a government facility in northern Kuwait. No casualties were reported.

Separate incidents also hit commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said an unidentified projectile struck a tanker on Friday about 11 nautical miles (20 kilometers) northeast of Lima, Oman, damaging its engine room.

On Saturday, another tanker reported a large splash and an explosion nearby while sailing around 21 nautical miles northwest of Khasab.

No casualties were reported in either maritime incident.

Iran has repeatedly targeted vessels attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz without its authorization during the conflict with the United States.

Skip next section Houthis claim Saudi oil shipments diverted

Houthis claim Saudi oil shipments diverted

Yemen's Houthi movement says eight Saudi oil tankers have been pushed off their usual routes as part of a newly declared blockade targeting the kingdom's energy exports.

According to the Iran-backed group, the ships will now have to make the much longer journey around South Africa's Cape of Good Hope to reach Asian markets.

Riyadh has not confirmed that any tankers were diverted.

The Houthis announced the blockade last week, framing it as retaliation for what they describe as years of Saudi pressure on Houthi-held parts of Yemen.

The group controls much of northern Yemen, including the capital Sanaa, after seizing territory in 2014 and setting off a war that drew in a Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognized government.

A major concern for global shipping is the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the narrow passage between Yemen and the Horn of Africa that links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

Any serious disruption there would add to pressure on trade routes already affected by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

The Houthis said they do not intend to levy transit charges on vessels using the strait.

Skip next section Iran warns regional states against helping US

Iran warns regional states against helping US

Iran's military has accused the United States of "escalating tensions" in the Middle East and warned regional neighbors against supporting Washington during the conflict.

"The United States is rapidly moving down the path of escalating tensions in the region," Ali Abdollahi, head of Iran's military central command, said in a statement broadcast on state television on Saturday.

"Any country serving as [a] defensive shield for criminal and aggressive America will be engulfed by the flames of war," he added.

The warning came after US President Donald Trump again threatened to hit Iran "very hard."

US media reported that Trump was considering renewed large-scale strikes as early as this weekend, potentially including attacks on energy infrastructure.

Iran and the United States resumed exchanges of fire this week after several days of relative calm, although no strikes were reported overnight from Friday into Saturday.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to DW's coverage of the situation in Iran and wider Middle East.

After US President Donald Trump again threatened to hit Iran, the head of Iran's military central command accused Washington of "escalating tensions" in the region.

Elsewhere, Yemen's Houthi movement says it has forced eight Saudi oil tankers away from their usual routes as part of a new blockade targeting the kingdom's energy exports.

Stay tuned for more news and analysis. For our previous day coverage of the conflict and the wider Middle East on July 31, 2026, you can catch our blog here.

entries.title: Greece battles wildfires, including near Athens
entries.summary: Firefighters were battling blazes in over 70 locations across Greece. Strong winds continue to fan the flames, adding to the firefighters' struggles.
entries.content:
Europe

Greece battles wildfires, including near Athens

August 1, 2026

Firefighters were battling blazes in over 70 locations across Greece. Strong winds continue to fan the flames, adding to the firefighters' struggles.

A raging wildfire has continued to engulf a popular coastal resort in Greece, even as hundreds of firefighters battle to put it out amid gusty winds.

The fire broke out on Friday near the coastal village of Agios Vasileios.

More than 300 firefighters have been deployed to control the wildfire, in an effort to prevent it from spreading to the area of Porto Germeno, some 70 kilometres (45 miles) northwest of Athens in the region of Viotia.

"The fire has reached the sea... homes have certainly been damaged," a fire department spokesman told the French AFP news agency.

"The winds are very strong. Aircraft are trying to operate as best they can, but some are unable to and have been transferred to another fire (in the Peloponnese) where conditions are milder," he added.

Winds up to 130 kilometres per hour, recorded on Saturday by the weather service of the National Observatory of Athens, have made the fire department's efforts more difficult.

"The environmental damage is huge," the mayor of Thebes, Giorgos Anastasiou, told Open TV.

Fire breaks out in several places across Greece

Wildfires have flared in several parts of the country this week, with  more than 70 locations in Greece affected by Friday.

The Greek fire brigade said it was at the maximum level of alert, warning that the fire risk was particularly high in the Attica peninsula and in Evia, an island east ‌of Athens where fires are frequent.

"The fire has reached the sea... homes have certainly been damaged," a fire department spokesman told AFP.

Theodore Giannaros, a wildfire meteorologist and senior researcher at the National Observatory of Athens on Saturday said the damage to the Porto Germeno area was "inconceivable."

Wildfires have raged in several parts of Greece this week, including the popular island of Crete, affecting some 5,000 hectares on the island. Three firefighters have lost their lives so far.

Several European countries have been battling savage wildfires this summer, amid extreme heatwaves and little rain.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: War in Ukraine: Why Crimea has become a strategic target
entries.summary: Ukraine has stepped up attacks on Russian logistics centers and energy facilities in Crimea. What are the consequences for local supplies, and how does Kyiv hope this strategy will affect the course of the war?
entries.content:
Ukraine

War in Ukraine: Why Crimea has become a strategic target

August 1, 2026

Ukraine has stepped up attacks on Russian logistics centers and energy facilities in Crimea. What are the consequences for local supplies, and how does Kyiv hope this strategy will affect the course of the war?

In an attempt to isolate Crimea from the mainland, the Ukrainian armed forces have intensified their attacks on the peninsula, which was invaded and annexed by Russia in 2014.

Ukraine is using long-range drones to attack transports on the M14 highway between the Russian city of Rostov-on-Don and Melitopol in occupied southern Ukraine. It is also targeting Russian shadow fleet ships in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea, as well as energy facilities that supply the Russian military.

Robert "Magyar" Brovdi, commander of the Ukrainian forces for unmanned systems, says 196 Russian ships and more than 100 energy facilities have been hit in the past month alone. His figures cannot be independently verified.

Russia appears to be struggling to supply both its military and the civilian population in Crimea. Fuel coupons were issued at the end of May, but ran out after 24 hours, after which gasoline was being traded on the black market. A state of emergency was declared in Crimea, especially Sevastopol, in response to repeated disruption of the electricity and water supply, and of the internet and cellphone networks.

What are residents in Crimea experiencing?

Nina, a pensioner who lives in a village near Feodosiya, southeastern Crimea, told DW about the difficulties people there are facing: Residents there can't cook because of power cuts, and fuel shortages mean public transport only runs intermittently. Nina's worst fear, though, is not having electricity in winter.

The longest power cuts have been in the north of Crimea. This is where Ivan lives [name changed]. He tells DW that for some time, people were unable to get hold of fuel with either coupons or cash. The only exceptions, he says, were police officers, state officials, and doctors. For several days, everything collapsed: Cars ran out of fuel and simply came to a stop; people didn't know how they were supposed to get to where they were going.

Ivan said that most shops no longer stock perishable goods, because they can't run their fridges and freezers: "There are no milk products, or fish, or meat," he said. "There are only a few shops with electricity generators, but the prices there are much higher than before."

Some small, private, volunteer initiatives are trying to help. The blogger Olena Gerasimenko works with companies in Simferopol to bring drinking water to people suffering from power cuts, and to hospitals and kindergartens. In her blog, she reports that people are complaining about the lack of help from the Russian-installed "authorities" in Crimea.

On social media, people say that, because of the power cuts and having no means of communication, residents of northern Crimea are sending post by public bus. But the buses aren't running regularly either.

What are Ukraine's tactics?

Ukraine's efforts to block supply routes both in and to Crimea are directed primarily against the small Russian tankers and tugboats that transport oil to larger ships and fuel to the Crimean mainland. Parallel to this, it is also destroying transformer substations. But Commander Brovdi says Ukraine is deliberately sparing the Kerch Bridge, which spans the Kerch Strait, connecting the peninsula with the Russian region of Krasnodar.

In a recent interview with the Irish journalist Caolan Robertson, Brovdi said the road and rail bridge should be maintained as a corridor for people to escape from Crimea. The aim is not to destroy it, Brovdi says, but to cut off Russian troops from supplies and reinforcements. "We want to make it impossible for the Russian military machine to remain and continue to operate there."

The military expert Ivan Kyrychevskyi serves in a Ukrainian drone unit. Speaking to DW he emphasized how important the air attacks on Crimea are for the frontline on the ground. "To stop the Russians getting anywhere near Zaporizhzhia, they have to put pressure on their lines of communication in the occupied south of Ukraine. This applies above all to Crimea. The blockade of shipping traffic in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea essentially has the same objective," says Kyrychevskyi. "For far too long, Crimea has served the Russians as a tranquil harbor and unsinkable aircraft carrier from which to carry out their offensives in southern Ukraine."

Pavlo Narozhnyi, a Ukrainian military expert and founder of the charitable organization Reactive Post, describes Crimea as a massive military base. Russian troops in the regions of Kherson and Zaporizhzhia are heavily dependent on it. Narozhnyi says that for a long time Russian logistics primarily ran through the peninsula, but this supply source is now being cut off on two sides: On land by attacks on the M14 highway, and at sea by attacks on transport vessels near the Crimea Bridge. "This way we are not isolating only Crimea but also the Russian troops in the south of Ukraine," Narozhnyi told DW. His organization supplies life-saving equipment to Ukrainian artillery divisions on the frontline.

Situation 'no worse' than in Ukrainian cities3

Narozhnyi explains that, at present, up to three million people in Crimea depend on Russia for their supplies. "A thermal power station that provided up to 60% of Crimea's entire electricity supply has been destroyed. The supply of oil products has been interrupted. The population is already experiencing problems, even with everyday things." The military expert also warned that these problems will get even worse in the fall, when the weather turns colder and people want to heat their homes. "Putin will then have to deal not only with military problems, but also the problems of the population," Narozhnyi says.

According to Sidharth Kaushal of the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) in London, attacks on power stations do not automatically contravene international law, particularly if the facilities have military significance and the attacks comply with the rule of proportionality.

Ukrainian experts confirm that the targeted facilities primarily supply electricity for military facilities. Kaushal told DW that he assumed a large-scale blockade strategy by Ukraine could ultimately compel Moscow to negotiate a ceasefire.

Commander Brovdi is asking people to be patient. "I apologize to the residents of Crimea, the Ukrainians, for the current difficulties. They are experiencing restrictions of advantages they have enjoyed all their lives – the supply of energy, water, and communications. But they are in a situation no worse than that of people in Kharkiv, Dnipro, Sumy, Zaporizhzhia, Nikopol, Kherson, and hundreds of other cities that are targeted on a daily basis."

This article was originally written in Ukrainian.

entries.title: How crypto miners are stealing power in Southeast Asia
entries.summary: Across Southeast Asia, illegal cryptocurrency miners are stealing vast amounts of electricity, straining national grids, and exposing links to organized crime.
entries.content:
August 1, 2026

Across Southeast Asia, illegal cryptocurrency miners are stealing vast amounts of electricity, straining national grids, and exposing links to organized crime.

A raid in Malaysia last week exposed how cryptocurrency mining is becoming entangled with electricity theft and organized crime across Southeast Asia.

In Malaysia's southern state of Johor, 71 cryptocurrency-mining machines had been running around the clock across four rented premises for about a month before police moved in.

During the raids on July 22 and 23, officers arrested three suspects and seized computers, routers and vehicles alongside equipment used to illegally mine Bitcoin. 

Johor police chief Ab Rahaman Arsad said the syndicate bypassed electricity meters, leading to an estimated €14,500 ($16,600) in losses in about a month, according to local media reports. The machines were thought to be generating between €17,200 and €21,500 in monthly revenue.

The case was relatively small by Malaysian standards. Between 2020 and 2025, national utility Tenaga Nasional Berhad (TNB) identified almost 14,000 premises linked to electricity theft for cryptocurrency mining. Its cumulative losses reached around €1.1 billion.

Recorded cases of such theft increased from 610 in 2018 to 2,397 in 2024, according to Malaysia's Energy Ministry, which has described illegal mining as a serious threat to public safety, economic stability, and the national electricity system.

"In Malaysia, thousands of incidents have triggered investigations into illegal mining for cryptocurrency purposes," said Sonny Zulhuda, associate professor at the International Islamic University Malaysia.

"This poses a huge problem for the security of electricity resources, economic sustainability, competition, and revenue loss," Zulhuda told DW. "Enforcement has been lagging behind, due to a lack of legislative preparedness and limited agency capability in enforcement and investigation. This is unfortunate because Malaysia is fast developing its digital infrastructure."

Where crypto mining meets organized crime

Cryptocurrency mining is not inherently criminal, but authorities are increasingly finding links between illegal crypto mining, online gambling, money laundering, and Southeast Asia's industrial-scale cyber scam networks.

Last October, the United States and the UK sanctioned the Cambodia-based Prince Group and associated companies, alleging that the network operated forced-labor scam compounds and laundered proceeds through cryptocurrencies and other assets.

US authorities also seized Bitcoin worth around $15 billion at the time from wallets whose private keys were held by Prince Group chairman Chen Zhi, describing the cryptocurrency as proceeds and instruments of fraud and money laundering.

Thailand's Department of Special Investigation has made the clearest connection between stolen electricity and transnational crime.

In 2025, investigators dismantled three major illegal crypto mining networks, seized more than 6,390 machines and estimated losses to the Provincial Electricity Authority at more than €24.9 million.

In one operation, authorities found around 1,900 mining machines at warehouse sites. The electricity authority estimated that the network was consuming power worth around €575,000 each month while paying only a fraction of the amount due.

Indonesia battles crypto mining crimes as well

Indonesia has seen similar cases. In December 2023, police in the province of North Sumatra raided ten sites and seized more than 1,100 Bitcoin-mining machines. State utility PLN estimated losses over six months at around €700,000.

Governments have responded with raids, tougher penalties and cooperation between police, utilities, regulators and anti-corruption agencies. Malaysia has created a multi-agency committee and deployed smart meters at substations to identify abnormal consumption. 

But enforcement remains difficult. Equipment can be moved quickly, premises can be rented through intermediaries and meter tampering may involve organized networks or insider assistance.

Saaidal Razalli Azzuhri, a telecommunications expert at the University of Malaya, told DW that raids should be supported by transformer-level monitoring, mandatory licensing, disclosure of companies' beneficial owners, and investigations tracing bank transfers and cryptocurrency wallets.

"The objective should not be to prohibit blockchain technology, but to ensure that miners pay the full economic cost of their electricity and do not transfer their costs and infrastructure risks to the public," he said.

Zulhuda said that Southeast Asian governments need to deal with this issue properly so they don't send the wrong message to companies that want to invest in the region's growing digital sectors.

Malaysia has several laws to curb illegal cyber activities, including the Cyber Security Act 2024 to protect its National Critical Information Infrastructure and the recently enacted Cybercrimes Act 2026 to address digital system misuse and abuse, he added.

Laos pulls the plug

Laos shows that even legal, state-backed cryptocurrency mining can struggle to deliver the promised benefits.

In mid-2021, the government authorized six companies to mine and trade cryptocurrencies. The plan appeared suited to a country that had invested heavily in hydropower and sometimes produced more electricity than its economy could absorb. Mining offered a way to monetize surplus energy.

At its peak in 2021 and 2022, the industry consumed around 500 megawatts. But the surplus proved unreliable.

Some miners accumulated unpaid bills. More importantly, officials concluded that the industry created few jobs and little demand for domestic suppliers compared with manufacturing or other commercial activities.

Deputy Energy Minister Chanthaboun Soukaloun said last October that the government intended to end electricity supplies to miners.

Laos wants to redirect the power towards metals processing, electric-vehicle manufacturing and artificial intelligence data centers, while increasing electricity exports to neighboring countries.

The experiment offered a broader warning. Cheap electricity can attract crypto miners, but it does not guarantee lasting investment or wider development. When operators steal power, or consume subsidized electricity without creating much value, the public is left carrying the cost.

Edited by Keith Walker

entries.title: Ceuta: Spain demands EU meeting, blasts 'selfish' response
entries.summary: After Italy temporarily suspended the Schengen deal with Spain, Spanish PM Pedro Sanchez said his county was being "attacked" from within the EU, stressing that Madrid fully restored control over its border. DW has more.
entries.content:
Published July 31, 2026last updated August 1, 2026

After Italy temporarily suspended the Schengen deal with Spain, Spanish PM Pedro Sanchez said his county was being "attacked" from within the EU, stressing that Madrid fully restored control over its border. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Italy's one-month suspension of the free-movement Schengen deal takes effect
  • Spain's Sanchez calls for an urgent teleconference of EU interior ministers
  • Madrid says 67 people died in the Ceuta mass incursion from Morocco
  • DW correspondent says thousands of migrants still in Ceuta
  • Germany's Merz calls on Morocco to take back the irregular migrants 'without delay' 

Follow this blog for continuing coverage and updates on the developing situation in Ceuta, Spain's North African territory.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Emergency meeting of European interior ministers to take place Tuesday

Emergency meeting of European interior ministers to take place Tuesday

An emergency video meeting of European Union interior ministers is to be held on Tuesday, according to Ireland's prime minister, Micheal Martin.

"As Presidency holders, Ireland will convene a meeting on Tuesday of the EU Justice and Home Affairs Council... to discuss developments in Ceuta," the Irish leader wrote on Saturday.

The Republic of Ireland currently holds the EU's rotating presidency and Irish Justice, ​Home ⁠Affairs and Migration Minister ⁠Jim O'Callaghan has been tapped by Martin to lead the call. 

Skip next section EU's von der Leyen says lessons must be learned to improve resilience

EU's von der Leyen says lessons must be learned to improve resilience

In a social media post on X, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she had "offered support to Spain from the first moment" and that most of those who stormed the Spanish North African enclave of Ceuta this week had been returned to Morocco.

"Not a single person reached mainland Spain or the rest of Europe," she said.

The head of the EU's executive said, however, that the bloc's "strong system" of border protections "needs to be further strengthened."

While emphasizing coordination, she said lessons must be learned "to improve our European resilience."

 

Calling for vigilance and coordination, von der Leyen ended her statement by saying, "Fighting illegal migration requires solidarity and a united European response."

Skip next section France says no need for Spain to leave Schengen

France says no need for Spain to leave Schengen

French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez on Saturday was cited by news agency AFP as saying that despite France's own increased security along its shared border with Spain, "We are not asking for Spain's suspension from Schengen."

Addressing calls by European politicians for Spain to be temporarily booted from the freedom of travel agreement, Nunez said: "Spain does not need to leave the Schengen zone. It's absolutely not on the table. We have great cooperation with Spain."

Italy announced a one-month suspension of visa-free movement with Spain on Friday after tens of thousands of migrants stormed the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, overwhelming authorities.

Spain has assured EU partners that irregular entry into Ceuta does not confer a right to remain in Spain, travel to the mainland, or move freely throughout Europe.

Skip next section DW reporter: Ceuta locals feel 'a mix of of fear and anger'

DW reporter: Ceuta locals feel 'a mix of of fear and anger'

DW correspondent Jan-Philipp Scholz reported high tensions in Ceuta on Saturday morning, despite the claims by the Spanish authorities that the situation in the exclave was back under control.

"I've still seen clashes between police, military and migrants, also between locals and some migrants this morning," he said.

While the overwhelming majority of irregular migrants has already left the area, Scholz pointed out that thousands were still in Ceuta and Spanish authorities were growing "increasingly robust" in their efforts to get the rest to leave. Most migrants did not receive any food or water, and all the shops in the area are closed, Scholz pointed out.

"They are pushing the people away from the beaches or from overwhelmed reception centers that cannot take any more people in," he said.

He also said that locals were feeling "a mix of fear and anger" in the wake of the incursion.

"Most people did not want to come out of their houses yesterday. And most people are still staying inside today."

Skip next section WATCH: Could the Ceuta crisis help Trump in the midterms?

WATCH: Could the Ceuta crisis help Trump in the midterms?

Donald Trump has called the migrant crossings into Spain an "invasion." US political analyst Michael Yaki unpacks the political strategy behind the rhetoric.

Skip next section IN PICTURES: Some migrants tell DW they don't want to go back to Morocco

IN PICTURES: Some migrants tell DW they don't want to go back to Morocco

Skip next section Spanish police start installing floating barrier

Spanish police start installing floating barrier

In Ceuta, Spanish authorities started laying a new pneumatic barrier on the sea border with Morocco.

The 500-meter (1,640-feet) long barrier is designed to stand 30 to 70 centimeters (12-28 ​inches) above the water line and up to one meter (3.3 feet) below it. It will run parallel to a line of anchored buoys, forming a channel that would be patrolled by Spanish law enforcement.

Many of the migrants that entered the Spanish territory of Ceuta in recent days achieved that by simply swimming around the existing barrier with Morocco and gaining access to the Spanish-controlled beach.

Spain's El Mundo daily published a video online of a Guardia Civil boat installing the barrier.

Skip next section Most EU nations join call for emergency talks after Ceuta crisis

Most EU nations join call for emergency talks after Ceuta crisis

In an open letter, 22 out of the EU's 27 members demanded a video meeting of the bloc's interior ministers on Saturday.

The meeting should be convened "as a matter of urgency" to coordinate a joint response to the situation in Ceuta, and "prevent further uncontrolled crossings."

Earlier on Saturday, Spain's Pedro Sanchez also called for a meeting of interior ministers.

Skip next section Sanchez: Spain managed to 'fully restore control of the border'

Sanchez: Spain managed to 'fully restore control of the border'

In less than 48 hours following the border incursion in Ceuta, the Spanish government has managed to "fully restore control of the border, provide extensive humanitarian aid, repatriate virtually all migrants who crossed irregularly, and prevent any unauthorized movement toward continental Europe," according to Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez.

"This has been achieved in close coordination with Moroccan authorities and with very little support from other European states," he added in the letter addressed to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and other top EU officials.

He also pointedly noted that Spain was "one of the European Union's least porous external borders, with a number of irregular entries that is half of that recorded in Italy in recent years (2021–2026), for example."

The Spanish leader also expressed confidence that a meeting of EU interior ministers would help "establish a common response to situations of this kind and reaffirm that the security of our external borders is a responsibility shared by all member states, and not just by those on the Union's front lines."

Skip next section Spain's Sanchez decries 'selfish' response by other EU nations

Spain's Sanchez decries 'selfish' response by other EU nations

The head of Spain's left-leaning government, Pedro Sanchez, demanded a video summit of all European Union interior ministers and slammed what he described as a "selfish" response by some EU members to the Ceuta crisis.

"Most have shown us their support and solidarity and have offered us their assistance. Others, however, have chosen to attack Spain and call for its temporary exclusion from the Schengen zone" Sanchez said, in apparent reference to Italy, which temporarily suspended free movement with Spain.

Denmark and Finland also called for reconsidering Spain's participation in the Schengen agreement, while Portugal and France responded by beefing up border security.

"In the current international context, the European Union cannot afford this kind of selfish, polarizing and unlawful reaction," Sanchez said in a letter to top EU leaders.

Skip next section Migrants in Ceuta boarding buses, trains back to Morocco

Migrants in Ceuta boarding buses, trains back to Morocco

With no means to reach mainland Spain or stay in the African exclave of Ceuta, thousands of migrants were going back into Morocco on Friday and Saturday.

A Moroccan source cited by the French AFP news agency said the migrants would either return by bus or be taken to a train station in Morocco's Tangier, some 70 kilometers (45 miles) away from Ceuta.

"I heard that buses had arrived to take us back home. Honestly, I just want to see my children again. I regret having come all the way here," said 32-year-old Moroccan Rachid Aouchari.

At the same time, some of the migrants in Ceuta told DW they wanted to stay.

"And I want food. I have four days [without food]," one of them said "Nothing, nothing. Just drinking water and no food."

"I don't want to go back to Morocco because I don't have anything in Morocco. Why would I want to go?"

Skip next section Spain faces diplomatic fallout as France and Italy respond to Ceuta incursion

Spain faces diplomatic fallout as France and Italy respond to Ceuta incursion

Italy has officially suspended the Schengen agreement with Spain on Saturday for one month in response to the mass crossing in Ceuta.

The Schengen deal allows for free movement between nearly all of the EU's 27 member states and several others that are not a part of the bloc, such as Switzerland, Norway and Iceland. It technically includes Spain’s exclaves such as Ceuta and Melilla, but passengers are still required to pass identity checks before traveling to Europe.

Even so, many EU nations responded with alarm following the news of thousands of irregular migrants pouring into Ceuta from Morocco.

Italy's far-right Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has described the images coming from Ceuta as "shocking." She said the Schengen agreement suspension is an "extraordinary measure" intended to "safeguard national security and prevent possible repercussions for our nation."

It is unclear how the temporary suspension will be implemented on the ground.

France, which shares a land border with Spain, boosted checks and deployed hundreds of additional law enforcement officers to the border by Saturday. At the same time, France's President Emmanuel Macron pledged solidarity and offered assistance to Spain.

Meanwhile, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez seemed to hit back at critics online, saying that solidarity and empathy were "optional" but " [r]espect for European treaties… is not."

Skip next section Spain updates Ceuta death toll to 67, says new barrier will be installed

Spain updates Ceuta death toll to 67, says new barrier will be installed

The death toll from the border collapse in Spain has been climbing since the incursion started on Thursday, with Spanish officials saying 67 bodies have been found by Saturday morning.

Spanish authorities also pledged to build a new containment barrier along the breakwater fence and into the sea for more security.

Skip next section Thousands of migrants still in Ceuta, DW correspondent reports

Thousands of migrants still in Ceuta, DW correspondent reports

Reporting from the scene in Ceuta, DW's Jan-Philipp Scholz says Spanish police and military were still out in force, and many irregular migrants remain in the Spanish exclave.

"Hundreds of migrants have spent the night on the beaches. Even though 80% to 90% have returned, there are still thousands of migrants in the exclave," he said.

"The migrants here still complain of hunger and thirst and are trying to get water at the beach showers," the DW correspondent added. "I'm also still hearing reports of some clashes with locals."

Skip next section We are resuming our coverage

We are resuming our coverage

We wish you a good Saturday morning from Bonn, with Europe still reeling from the Ceuta border collapse. The Spanish exclave in Africa has seen some 60,000 people rush through the border from Morocco and gain entry to the Spanish city of some 85,000 residents.

While most of the irregular migrants reportedly returned to Morocco by Saturday morning, the incursion sparked alarm over the free-movement Schengen zone, with Italy even suspending the deal with Spain for one month.

Meanwhile, France boosted border checks with Spain while also pledging solidarity and offering assistance to Pedro Sanchez's government.

The incident has inflamed the already bitter political divide on migration within the EU.

We will be bringing you more on this story, including reports from our reporter in Ceuta, throughout the day.

entries.title: Germany weighs the future of minijobs
entries.summary: Germany's popular minijob system allows millions of workers, including students, to avoid paying income tax or social security contributions. But a reform is on the cards that may soon end this advantage.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany weighs the future of minijobs

August 1, 2026

Germany's popular minijob system allows millions of workers, including students, to avoid paying income tax or social security contributions. But a reform is on the cards that may soon end this advantage.

When Anahita Abdollahi starts her shift, she first checks her emails to make sure she's up to date on all the library requests. The 26-year-old master's student from Iran describes her job as a "part-time librarian" — she helps people find books they need for their studies, answers phone calls, and waters the plants.  

Abdollahi says she likes "almost everything" about her job at the University of Cologne's physics library — the only exception is the occasional tedious task, such as taking inventory of the library's collection. But even that doesn't bother her too much — after all, she only works twice a week for around five hours at a time. 

This type of employment is known in Germany as a "minijob", whichthe country's government is considering eliminating in its current form. 

Minijobs popular with women and students

A minijob is a form of part-time employment in Germany which pays a maximum of €603 (around $685) per month. As long as employees don't earn more than this amount, they don't have to pay social insurance contributions or income tax.

Minijobbers can also opt out of paying their share of pension contributions — and most of them do just that.

A minijobber typically works around 10 hours per week to reach the €603 cap, making it an ideal job for those with other commitments, such as students or stay-at-home parents. Women make up around 57% of all minijobbers, according to Germany's central agency for minijobs.

The agency also estimates that nearly 7 million of Germany's 45 million employees have a minijob. Some of them have it in addition to another job, while others have a minijob as their only form of employment.

Minijobs were introduced in the 1960s to facilitate low-level employment with little bureaucracy and to combat moonlighting. In 2003, they were redesigned as part of a comprehensive labor market reform.

They have long been criticized for reinforcing gender inequality in the job market, as minijobs are held disproportionately often by women, preventing them from building up substantial pensions. 

What are the benefits for employers?

Employers typically pay a flat tax of 2% on minijobbers' wages, as well as social contributions amounting to around 30% of gross pay. Despite these additional costs, many businesses rely on minijobbers because they offer flexibility.

"There are operational situations where hiring someone only makes sense if the number of hours is truly minimal," Holger Schäfer, a senior economist specializing in labor market economics at the German Economic Institute (IW), told DW.

Supermarkets, for example, need more cashiers on Saturday afternoons than they do on Monday mornings, making minijobs an easy way to fill the staffing gap. The extra weekend work is also why retail and hospitality are the two industries that employ the most minijobbers.

How could minijobs change?

In early July, Germany's governing coalition announced its plans to raise the flat tax rate for minijobs from 2% to 5%. The government also stated its intention to fully implement the Pension Commission's proposals, which were presented in late June and aim to ensure the sustainability of Germany's pension system in the future. 

One of these proposals focuses specifically on minijobs, and would eliminate the opt-out option for pension contributions and abolish the special status of minijobs. This would make minijobbers subject to regular social security contributions, effectively bringing an end to minijobs in their current form. According to the commission, this would strengthen social security systems, reduce the risk of poverty in old age, and address gender inequalities.

For Abdollahi, it could mean earning up to €130 less per month. The 26-year-old says she would probably try to increase her work hours to make up for the loss.

She could also get a research job that would require her to work for up to 20 hours per week, but this would considerably slow down the pace of her studies. "Even with my admittedly very chill job here, on the days I work, I usually don't study," Abdollahi explained.

How is the proposal being received?

Many labor unions have welcomed the proposal, including Nahrung-Genuss-Gaststätten (NGG), a trade union representing workers in the food, beverage, catering, and hospitality industries.  

"Minijobs have not proven to be a bridge to good employment; rather, they cement precarious working conditions for millions of people," the NGG cited their chairman Guido Zeitler in a press statement.  

Enzo Weber, a labor market expert from the Institute for Employment Research (IAB), believes the reform may encourage people to work more or pursue different career paths. It would "prevent people from getting stuck in the minijob trap" and "ensure that women's career development doesn't stall during child-rearing years, since they simply remain in low-paying jobs due to misguided tax incentives," Weber told DW.

Business representatives, however, have pushed back against the proposed changes. "Abolishing minijobs would be a mistake," argued Rainer Dulger, president of the Federal Association of German Employers' Organizations, adding that minijobs help businesses remain flexible and tap into additional labor potential. 

IW economist Schäfer, meanwhile, doubts that abolishing minijobs would encourage people to work significantly more hours. He also notes that a €600 job fully subject to social security contributions would generate rather small additional benefits. "It's simply not worth it to set the entire social security machinery in motion for such employment relationships," Schäfer said.

Still, he sees room for reform when it comes to people who take on a minijob alongside their primary employment. "We have an economic misallocation of resources when a skilled worker would rather deliver pizza after work than work overtime in their actual main job," he explained. "But that doesn't mean we have to abolish minijobs altogether."

Exemptions for university students?

The Pension Commission's proposals also include an exemption for school students, which would allow them to continue working minijobs in their current form. Now, the Social Democratic Party (SPD) is considering whether this exemption could be extended to university students. 

Abdollahi believes that would be the right decision. "They are one of the groups that need it the most, especially students from outside the EU," she said.

Abdollahi's own minijob at the library allowed her to enter the German labor market more easily and helped her improve her language skills. "It gives me a chance to practice German in a low-pressure environment," she noted.

But Abdollahi and other students in Germany now have to wait to learn what will happen to minijobs, as the government is expected to debate the proposed changes later this year.

Edited by Rina Goldenberg

Sami Behbehani contributed to this report.
